title: Cap. VI Arg. 3: Prosper, Hilary, Faustus — election-on-faith always meant prior merit
pass_a_gloss: Nor does Augustine alone argue that that benefit is given from merit which is given from a preceding condition of faith, but (what is worthy of note) whoever of old suspended election to life upon the condition of faith thereby acknowledged an antecedent dignity and merit in the elect. So Prosper in the Letter to Augustine, where he expounds the opinion of those who were called the remnants of the Pelagians: As far as concerns God, they say eternal life is prepared for all; but as far as concerns free choice, it is apprehended by those who have spontaneously believed God, and have received the help of grace by the merit of believing. So also Hilary writing to Augustine on the same matter shows that those who rejected election according to God's purpose, and introduced election according to foresight of faith and penitence, acknowledged in this faith and conversion the merit and cause of election: By that merit by which they have willed and believed they can be healed of their disease, etc. And a little later, If any grief whatsoever arises, they say this very thing is the cause on account of which one is taken and another rejected. Finally Faustus of Riez, who most carefully defends the Semi-Pelagian opinion, as he establishes election from foresighted faith, so also does not dissemble that the same is done from merit: Foreknowledge, he says, knows beforehand what is to be done; afterwards predestination describes what is to be retributed; the one foresees merits, the other preordains rewards. Too subtle therefore are the Remonstrants, and they desert their elders, when they set down that God elects men according to foresight of faith, and yet deny that foresighted faith is the cause of said election.
pass_b_english: Augustine is not alone: whoever of old hung election to life on a faith-condition thereby admitted prior dignity and merit in the elect. Prosper (Letter to Augustine), on the so-called Pelagian remnants: as far as God goes, eternal life is prepared for all; as far as free choice goes, it is grasped by those who spontaneously believed, and received grace help by the merit of believing. Hilary to Augustine: those who rejected election according to God's purpose and brought in election by foresight of faith and penitence recognized in that faith and conversion the merit and cause of election — by the merit of willing and believing they can be healed, and later, whatever grief arises, they call that the very cause why one is taken and another rejected. Faustus of Riez, careful Semi-Pelagian: as he grounds election in foresighted faith, so he does not hide that it is also from merit — Foreknowledge knows what will be done; predestination then describes the retribution; the one foresees merits, the other preordains rewards. Remonstrants are too clever, and desert their elders, when they have God elect by foresight of faith and still deny that foresighted faith is the cause.
source_text: Nec Augustinus solummodo arguit beneficium illud ex merito dari, quod datur ex fidei conditione praeeunte, sed (quod notatu dignum est) quicunque olim electionem ad vitam ex conditione fidei suspenderunt, inde dignitatem et meritum antecedaneum in electis agnoverunt. Sic Prosper in Epist. ad Augustinum, ubi exponit sententiam illorum qui reliquiae Pelagianorum appellabantur: Quantum ad Deum pertinet, omnibus paratam vitam aeternam esse dicunt; quantum autem ad arbitrii libertatem, ab his eam apprehendi qui Deo sponte crediderint, et auxilium gratiae merito credulitatis acceperint. Sic etiam Hilarius ad Augustinum scribens de eadem materia, ostendit eos qui rejiciebant electionem secundum Dei propositum, et introducebant electionem secundum fidei et paenitentiae praevisionem, in hac fide et conversione meritum et causam electionis agnovisse: Eo merito quo voluerint et crediderint a suo morbo se posse sanari, etc. Et Paulo post, Si qualiscunque dolor oriatur, hanc ipsam dicunt causam propter quam alius assumatur, alius rejiciatur. Denique Faustus Regiensis, qui accuratissime Semipelagianorum sententiam tutatur, sicut electionem ex fide praevisa statuit, ita etiam ex merito eandem fieri non dissimulat: Praescientia, inquit, gerenda praenoscit, postmodum praedestinatio retribuenda describit; illa praevidet merita, haec praeordinat praemia. Nimis igitur arguti sunt, et a majoribus suis desciscunt Remonstrantes, quando ponunt Deum eligere homines secundum praescientiam fidei, et tamen negant fidem praevisam esse causam dictae electionis.
